from manim import *
from pathlib import Path
import yaml

# Load style
with open("visual-style_dark.yml", "r", encoding="utf-8") as f:
    STYLE = yaml.safe_load(f)


%%manim -qm -v WARNING SimpleDiagram

class SimpleDiagram(Scene):
    def construct(self):

        self.camera.background_color = STYLE["canvas"]["background"]

        # Main object
        box = RoundedRectangle(
            width=3.2,
            height=1.6,
            corner_radius=STYLE["shapes"]["corners"]["large"],
            stroke_color=STYLE["strokes"]["color"]["primary"],
            stroke_width=STYLE["strokes"]["width"]["normal"],
            fill_color=STYLE["colors"]["palette"]["blue"]["light"],
            fill_opacity=STYLE["shapes"]["fill"]["soft_opacity"],
        )

        # Label
        label = Text(
            "System",
            font=STYLE["typography"]["fonts"]["sans"],
            font_size=STYLE["typography"]["sizes"]["label"],
            color=STYLE["typography"]["color"]["primary"],
        )

        # Input/output arrows
        arrow_style = dict(
            color=STYLE["arrows"]["color"],
            stroke_width=STYLE["arrows"]["stroke_width"],
            tip_length=STYLE["arrows"]["tip"]["length"],
            buff=0.15,
        )

        arrow_in = Arrow(
            LEFT * 4,
            box.get_left(),
            color=STYLE["arrows"]["color"],
            stroke_width=STYLE["arrows"]["stroke_width"],
            tip_length=STYLE["arrows"]["tip"]["length"],
            buff=0.15,
        )

        arrow_out = Arrow(
            box.get_right(),
            RIGHT * 4,
            color=STYLE["arrows"]["color"],
            stroke_width=STYLE["arrows"]["stroke_width"],
            tip_length=STYLE["arrows"]["tip"]["length"],
            buff=0.15,
        )

        input_text = Text(
            "Input",
            font=STYLE["typography"]["fonts"]["sans"],
            font_size=STYLE["typography"]["sizes"]["annotation"],
            color=STYLE["typography"]["color"]["secondary"],
        ).next_to(arrow_in, UP, buff=0.15)

        output_text = Text(
            "Output",
            font=STYLE["typography"]["fonts"]["mono"],
            font_size=STYLE["typography"]["sizes"]["annotation"],
            color=STYLE["typography"]["color"]["secondary"],
        ).next_to(arrow_out, UP, buff=0.15)

        self.add(
            box,
            label,
            arrow_in,
            arrow_out,
            input_text,
            output_text,
        )

title: Photonics Notes
text:
I am a Ph.D. student in Korea studying nanophotonics, a field that explores how light interacts with matter at sub-wavelength scales. This blog is a record of my journey through that field: what I learn, what confuses me, and how my understanding develops over time. The notes are built upon my understandings, with the assistance of research papers, lecture materials, textbooks, discussions, and of course, generative AI. My hope is that documenting the process of learning nanophotonics will be useful not only to me, but also to others exploring the same questions.

title: Author
text:
Ph.D. Candidate


School of Electrical Engineering and Computer Science, Korea Advanced Institute of Science and Technology (KAIST)


Google Scholar GitHub ORCID




Sunghyun (Felix) Nam


I’m a Ph.D. candidate in the research group of Prof. Min Seok Jang at KAIST’s School of Electrical Engineering. My research focuses on understanding and designing nanophotonic systems, with a particular interest in resonant metasurfaces and their underlying physics.
My name is 남성현 in Korean, and I go by Felix in English, which is also my Catholic baptismal name. I am currently in Boston, MA, visiting the Kiyoul Yang Research Group of Harvard University.


Research

My primary research interests lie in the theoretical and computational analysis and design of nanophotonic devices, with a particular focus on metasurfaces. I am especially interested in understanding the physical mechanisms that govern their optical response and using this understanding to guide the design of new photonic functionalities.
My research interests include, but are not limited to:

Design and physical interpretation of resonant metasurfaces, with an emphasis on modal analysis and forward design using temporal coupled-mode theory and quasinormal-mode theory.
Computational simulation and inverse design of metasurfaces, using numerical methods such as RCWA, FEM, and FDTD together with optimization techniques including gradient-based and adjoint methods
Machine-learning-assisted nanophotonics, particularly the use of machine learning for electromagnetic surrogate modeling, accelerated simulation, and photonic device optimization.


Academic Background



B.S. in Physics, KAIST Dual degree in Electrical Engineering, Magna Cum Laude March 2017 – February 2024


M.S. in Electrical Engineering, KAIST March 2024 – February 2026


Ph.D. in Electrical Engineering, KAIST March 2026 – Present



Experience



Research Intern, Jang Research Group June 2020 – July 2021


KATUSA, Republic of Korea Army Military Service November 2021 – May 2023


Visiting Scholar, Harvard John A. Paulson School of Engineering and Applied Sciences Kiyoul Yang Research Group July 2026 – December 2026



Beyond Research


Beyond spending my entire life in the lab, I am a veteran shortstop for the KAIST baseball team, a beginner sabre fencer, and a very shit golfer. I am also a avid fan of the Seoul LG Twins baseball team, Royal Blood, and Tchaikovsky.

title: Optical Resonances
text:
OPTICAL RESONANCES


Understanding resonant behavior in photonic systems.


This section collects my notes on optical resonances, from their basic physical interpretation to the mathematical frameworks used to describe resonant photonic systems.


What are optical resonances?
Optical, or more generally electromagnetic (EM), resonances arise when light is temporarily confined or strongly concentrated within a finite region of space rather than immediately scattering away through radiative channels. For a given photonic structure, resonances occur at particular frequencies where Maxwell’s equations and the electromagnetic boundary conditions support characteristic field patterns. Within these resonant states, electromagnetic energy oscillates between electric and magnetic forms while loss through radiative channels or material absorption is rather gradual. The extent to which a resonance can be excited from the outside depends additionally on properties of the incident light, such as its momentum and polarization[1].  These resonances appear as characteristic features in the optical response of a system, such as peaks or dips in experimentally measured transmission and reflection spectra. However, resonances carry a deeper physical meaning than the spectral feature through which it is observed. It represents an intrinsic electromagnetic state of the photonic system and therefore provides a fundamental description of how the structure stores, confines, and couples electromagnetic energy. In this sense, understanding the resonances of a photonic device provides a direct route to understanding its interaction with light.

[1]: Karavaev, I., et al., Newton (2026).



Why are optical resonances important?
Resonances are central to many optical devices because they allow strong electromagnetic effects to be produced within structures much smaller than the propagation distance that would otherwise be required. One important consequence is enhanced light–matter interaction. By concentrating electromagnetic energy in space and increasing the time over which the field interacts with a material, resonant structures can strongly enhance processes such as spontaneous emission, nonlinear frequency conversion including second- and third-harmonic generation, Raman scattering, absorption, sensing, and interactions with excitons or other quantum emitters. A second consequence is an enhanced effective optical path length. Light can undergo repeated interactions with a resonant structure even when the physical thickness of the device is deeply subwavelength. This makes it possible to obtain large changes in phase, amplitude, polarization, or absorption from relatively small changes in refractive index or material properties, which is particularly important for compact modulators and actively tunable photonic devices. A third important role is spectral and spatial selectivity. Resonances allow a device to interact strongly with selected frequencies, polarizations, propagation directions, or radiation channels while remaining weakly coupled to others. This selectivity forms the basis of narrowband filters, directional emitters, perfect absorbers, high-sensitivity sensors, and many metasurface functionalities.


How will we approach optical resonances?
There are several complementary ways to understand a resonant photonic system. We will first introduce a rigorous modal picture using quasinormal modes. Because realistic optical resonators are open systems that radiate energy into their surroundings, their natural modes generally possess complex eigenfrequencies. Quasinormal-mode analysis provides a direct connection between these complex eigenfrequencies, resonance lifetimes, quality factors, and the spatial electromagnetic fields of the resonator. We will then examine how these resonant modes interact with external radiation using temporal coupled-mode theory. Rather than focusing on the full electromagnetic field, temporal coupled-mode theory describes the exchange of energy between a small number of resonant modes and incoming or outgoing radiation channels. This framework makes concepts such as radiative decay, critical coupling, interference, and resonant scattering particularly transparent. Finally, we will study several important families of resonances encountered in nanophotonic systems. These include Mie resonances supported by individual dielectric particles, guided-mode and photonic-crystal resonances originating from periodic structures, and high-Q states such as bound states in the continuum and quasi-BICs. Photonic crystals will be especially important in this discussion because periodicity introduces Bloch modes and photonic band structures, providing another route to confine and manipulate electromagnetic waves and serving as the foundation for many guided resonances and BIC-based structures. Together, these viewpoints will let us move between three complementary questions: What is the resonant mode? How does it couple to the outside world? And what physical mechanism produces it in a particular photonic structure?
